learningObjectives: Recognize the fan-out anti-pattern: splitting a broad topic into 'one agent per file' or 'one agent per directory' as a way to give everyone something to do, rather than because the split changes the answer.

Apply the three-part fan-out test — few enough lots to name individually, genuinely disjoint territory, and each lot needing independently gathered evidence — before dispatching more than one agent on a task.
Distinguish a legitimate split by genuinely separate capability (different machines, different deployed engines) from the same corpus cut up for headcount.
State, for a proposed multi-agent split, the specific decision it would change versus the cost of running it as one sequential pass.
definitions: Fan-out anti-pattern: dispatching many agents against one corpus or topic in a way that looks thorough but does not change the answer any single sequential agent would have reached.
Disjoint lot: a scope of work that no other concurrently dispatched agent reads or writes, so two agents cannot silently overwrite each other.

Usage law: the standing house rule that prose or survey sweeps never fan out on a session's own initiative — an owner-ordered broad survey has already answered whether to fan out; what remains is sizing its named families correctly.
facilitationPlan: Live 90-minute session built around one named, dated incident: a word-sweep across a codebase spawned 8 parallel subagents on the session's own initiative while the engine itself had zero lines of code written — real tokens and real time spent on prose cleanup while the actual product sat unbuilt. Read the incident as recorded in the house working-discipline rule file. Then run the three-part fan-out test live against three prepared example tasks (one genuinely worth splitting, two disguised anti-patterns) and have the room vote and argue before revealing the intended answer. Close with participants applying the test to a broad task from their own backlog and writing the one sentence that names the decision a split would change — or the decision to do it as one agent instead.
humanFrame: More agents is not more thoroughness. Every additional dispatch has a real cost in tokens, time, and reconciliation effort; the question is never 'could I split this?' but 'does splitting this change what I would conclude?'
assessment: Given four candidate multi-agent dispatch plans, participants correctly classify each as a legitimate disjoint-evidence split or a disguised fan-out anti-pattern, and for each anti-pattern name the cheaper single-agent alternative.
